utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, before we start this morning, I think yesterday you tried to tell us something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank Your Honour for giving me the floor. And I apologize for having stopped you when you were leaving. I thought that there was something very urgent. We have, meanwhile, resolved the issue. I don't want to belabour it any longer. We just were able to resolve the issue after you left the courtroom yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I have to warn you that when the Judges are rising, you should not interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of this now, but I apologised right away. The point is that because we don't have enough communication with my client, I usually get little notes and I know what is going on with my client. So I am aware that I should not rise after the Court has adjourned, so I apologise one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Scott: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mrachacz.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, before we return and just to refresh the memories of all in the courtroom, we were talking about the shelling of a mosque in Mostar at the end of the day yesterday. However, before we pick up with that again, I'd like to go back, please, to two other topics briefly. Let me direct your attention, first of all, please, back to the incident where the tanker truck was placed into Mostar that you told us about, which exploded, and which you talked to the driver afterwards and were told that this was done on Tuta's order. Can you tell the Chamber, please, did you ever know other instances where Tuta used a similar practice or tactic, the use of fuel or gasoline as a weapon, if you will?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know of any instances that these things would have been used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can refresh your memory to a time with the attack on the Velez hill in 1992 against the Serbs. Do you remember gasoline being used on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a lot of losses, and the Serb units had withdrawn to their station. But Tuta only made a mention of the possibility that this bunker could be exploded by pouring gasoline in, but it was not practised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the final question on this point: Is it true or can you help the Chamber, is that something that Tuta discussed on a number of occasions? And by that, I mean the use of an exploding fuel, or gasoline, or a tanker, as something that he frequently discussed as a potential tactic.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, you have extensive knowledge of the structure and workings of the Convicts' Battalion, its command and its component parts, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard your question, but I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have extensive knowledge -- based on your long association, in fact, as an officer of the Convicts' Battalion, you have extensive knowledge of the structure and workings of the Convicts' Battalion and its components. True?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one couldn't say so. I am not informed about all the things. I had not been employed with the headquarters, so many things are just beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, and Mr. President, I'm going to submit that you demonstrated in your testimony yesterday an extensive knowledge of these topics, and I'm going to ask you if you recall -- based on that knowledge, do you recall anything more that you can tell us this morning about a component of the Convicts' Battalion that was based in Mostar City, if you will, not the Heliodrom, but based in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information about anything in Mostar itself, because I usually stayed in Siroki Brijeg. And I had no information and insight in what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed a written statement on the 17th of February, 1998, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that refresh your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I am aware in Mostar, that was the expelling of Muslims into the other side of Mostar. But how this has happened, I cannot make any statement. Members of our unit told me the very next day that they had participated in this action, but who was in charge of that and who gave the orders is beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, I appreciate that clarification. I truly do. But my question to you at the moment is: I am probing your memory about the basing of one of the other Convicts' Battalion components in the city of Mostar. So please, listen to my questions. You made a statement on the 17th of February, 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And concerning -- my apologies to Interpretation. And concerning this component in Mostar, if you reviewed your February 17th statement, 1998, might that refresh your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I cannot remember. I do not know what the statement was on that date. And what I remembered was based on hearsay, and, therefore, I cannot say whether this is completely in line with the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I'm going to ask you to provide this statement to the witness. Counsel, I am referring to Mr. Mrachacz's written statement taken on the 17th of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there are two things. First one is if we could get one, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the other thing is that I saw Mr. Meek is standing. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber, I believe that the Prosecutor is now attempting to impeach his own witness by putting forth to him statements that were allegedly given three years ago. I do not believe it is appropriate for the Prosecutor to impeach his own witness. There is no mechanism that I am aware of in this Trial Chamber or in this Tribunal to have any witness declared to be a hostile witness, number one. Secondly, I don't believe that this witness is a hostile witness. This witness has been attempting to answer questions to the best of his knowledge. Now the Prosecutor would like to put in front of this witness a statement allegedly given on the 17th of February, 1998, also distributing that statement to this Trial Chamber. This witness has already testified that he does not remember what he said, and his memory today would not be in line, perhaps, with that statement. In the fundamental principle of fairness or due process, the Defence is not able to cross-examine a document such as a statement of February 17th. And if you allow this procedure, the Defence will be prejudiced as we will not be able to confront the accusers against our client. We cannot examine or cross-examine a statement, and that is what you will have us in the position of. We will be put in that position if you allow this procedure. We object strongly to this procedure. This is not a hostile witness in any fashion. This witness is trying to truthfully answer the questions put to him, and it is unfortunate that the Prosecutor does not believe that the answers are what he desires. But just because the answers are not as he desires does not make this witness a hostile witness. And in fact, to allow this procedure would seriously damage the rights of this accused, my accused, Mr. Naletilic, to a fair trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think probably you could take your witness step by step rather than jump to that statement directly. You may ask a few questions whether he made the statement or not; and later on, you just take your witness to where it should be. And Judge Clark wants to make an intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to be able to state -- we haven't been afforded the opportunity of stating either our position or theory yet. I would appreciate being able to do that at some point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I agree entirely with the President. In the interests of justice and in pursuance of the rules of evidence, Rule 89, the Trial Chamber can admit or exclude any evidence which it deems to be unreliable. At the moment, we simply do not know. This witness may indeed not be of any assistance either to the Defence or to the Prosecution. But in the interest of justice, we feel that you ought to ask this witness, first of all, did he make the statement, and are the contents of that statement true? Depending on what he says there, I'm sure you'll take your own courses as to whether you wish to proceed at all with this witness. But that's a matter entirely for you, Mr. Scott. But in relation to you, Mr. Meek, you are concerned that this witness's evidence is being impugned. It's only a step to ascertain whether this should be so. And I know this hasn't come up in other cases. It's unusual. Most trials proceed without it happening, and it's in the interests of all of us to see just where we stand with this witness. Thank you. We just have to be a little patient with new procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I strongly disagree with my learned friend on the other side, and I must also disagree with the Chamber's statements. No one so far has properly stated our position or the position in which we are offering this evidence. And since we have not been heard yet, I would submit that it would be the more appropriate procedure that the Prosecution be heard and its position stated before further instructions are given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment I think there should be no translation to the witness, because we are doing legal argument concerning the Rules of Procedures rather than factual matters. So that's somehow to meet the request of Mr. Meek the other day. But that will be very extraordinary occasions, because we look into the Rules of Procedure and we look into the precedent of the Trial Chamber, as well as most of the practices in the world, if not all. There's no such kind of rules for barring the witness hearing the objections concerned with a leading question. But when the Trial Chamber is dealing with the legal issues, the witness should not be allowed to hear the contents. You understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand and I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court, the Prosecution is not attempting to impeach this witness. There are a number of steps that can be taken with the witness, as the Chamber will know, at least in the practice that I'm familiar with. We all come from different practices, and I believe the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this institution might be described as broadly inclusive, rather than exclusive, to admit the maximum amount, I would say, of allowable and probative evidence for the professional Judges of this Chamber to ultimately receive and consider and give weight to. There is no Rule against leading questions. There is no Rule against hearsay. There is no Rule against impeaching your own witness. The Rules provide a broad philosophy, if you will. Of course we want the proceedings to happen fairly and in a way that maximises the effective presentation of evidence. Absolutely, you would have no disagreement from the Prosecution on that. Having said all that, again I can only draw -- all of us, to some extent, can draw only on our past experiences, modified to the extent necessary to this institution, and sometimes very different practices than where we come from. Certainly, there is many different practices here than where I practise in the United States. But those are the practices here. In refreshing the witness's recollection, as we got into the other day and unfortunately there was an unfortunate misunderstanding, sometimes where I come from, if there is an evidence issue of recollection and the possibility of refreshing recollection, the judges will often give counsel some leeway to lead the witness, to see if the memory can be probed or refreshed. That's what I was attempting to do, which led to apparently some confusion on that point. Secondly, a witness's testimony can -- through various devices, the Prosecution or the Defence, if properly done, can seek to refresh the witness's recollection. It has nothing to do with impeachment. It is again called, where I come from, "refreshed recollection," and that is what I'm attempting to do. I did ask - the record will show this very clearly - I asked the witness first if he had made a statement, if he had made a statement. And he said, yes, he did, on February 17th, 1998. That's where we were and that's as far as we had gotten when Defence counsel took his feet and, before the Chamber, intervened. So I will try to go forward, try to follow at least the proper procedure that I'm familiar with. If the Chamber ultimately disagrees with that, you can certainly exclude it, you can certainly tell me not to pursue it. But that's what I'm trying to do, according to the procedure that I'm familiar with. I'm not seeking to impeach the witness. I'm seeking to refresh his recollection of the past statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Par standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a comment on what my learned friend from the Prosecution has just said. I would like to make a comment about what he said, refreshing the recollection. I know that in some situations, the Prosecutor needs to refresh the witness's recollection, but I think here we have a case of exerting pressure on the witness. We did not have any refreshing of recollection here, because the Prosecutor tried, with several questions, to get there but was unsuccessful. Following that, he asked the witness whether he had given some kind of a statement, and now he was going to show him, this witness -- and will show to the witness what he had said; in other words, to exert certain amount of pressure on him. I believe that if the intention of the Prosecutor was to refresh the witness's recollection, that there were ways to do so through questions. And he should have asked him first what he had stated in that statement, and then if there is some kind of discrepancy there or something, then he needs to put his statement to him and try to clarify matters. Here we had a case when the witness was immediately given the statement and so that he could read it and so that the answer which had been in the statement would be repeated by him. So in order not to belabour the point more, we believe that this was an undue pressure exerted on the witness, and I request that this manner of questioning be disallowed. I believe that the Prosecution has other ways of refreshing the witness's recollection, if they need to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, this was explored exactly as Mr. Par, my learned friend, just indicated, yesterday. And I went through these steps. There were questions about this component, and at that time he did not recall anything more. I took those preliminary steps. And once again, I've only been allowed so far to ask him if he made a statement. I haven't asked him to read anything. I haven't asked him to say anything. I haven't compelled him to say anything. I'm simply following a procedure, based on his testimony yesterday, the exhaustion of his recollection on this point, and tendering a document to see if it refreshes his recollection. And that is the procedure that I'm seeking to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My objection to that has already been noted. But the procedure logistically, I believe, is inappropriate if the Prosecutor, Mr. Scott, gets to the point where he needs to tender this alleged statement that was made three years ago to the witness to allow him to review it, to refresh his recollection. My issue and my point is that if that statement is given to the Trial Chamber at the same time it's given to the witness, and the witness is unable to remember making that statement, the Trial Chamber then has that statement, has read that statement. And again, I believe, as Judge Clark indicated, there are other ways in which to ask this witness and refresh this witness's recollection short of submitting the document to the witness. And further, again, submitting the document to the witness is one thing, but simultaneously submitting the same document to the finders of fact is a wholly different matter, in my opinion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, there should be an end to this debate. I've given you lots of chance to express your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can state that I'm in full agreement with Mr. Meek on one point, and that is I agree that, with all respect, the Judges shouldn't have the statement, and that would also be the practice where both Mr. Meek and I come from. It is not a matter of evidence. The document is not admitted into evidence. It is simply used as a memory-refreshing device. It is not evidence. And it does not go to the trier of fact. In my jurisdiction, it would not go to a jury and it would not go to a judge. And I would agree with Mr. Meek that you should not see it. It either refreshes the witness's memory or it does not. If he says no and has nothing further to add, that is the end of it. If it does refresh his memory, he will tell us whatever else he remembers. That is the procedure according to the book, as I recall it, again, from where I come from. If the Chamber decides it does not want to allow this practice to be done, I suppose that's your prerogative. I would think that would be the wrong position, but I think it's certainly your prerogative. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, after hearing the arguments from the both sides and after consultations among the Judges, we have decided that you may show the witness the statement he made three years ago to refresh his recollections. But I hope that the statement will be tendered into evidence at a certain stage if -- if -- if we find some probative value from the statement as well as the testimony by this witness. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you have the statement in front of you, sir -- and actually, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, it would be our position it should not be tendered to the Chamber, but that's up to you, Mr. President. Mr. Usher, I'm going to have to ask you, please, to recover that statement from the witness stand for the moment, please. Again, in all these steps, some of the steps have gotten a bit out of order. Can I ask the Registrar to give that a temporary identification number, please. This is a number only for identification purposes, for the record, Mr. President. It's not an indication at all that the document will be admitted or offered into evidence, but simply to identify it for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: ID Number 1. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Mr. Usher, could you please tender to the witness what has been marked only for identification purposes ID1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, the first thing I want you to do, please, is turn your attention to the fourth page of the document, and not necessarily -- the pages may not -- I think it does turn out to be the numbered page 4, also physically page 4 in the grouping of pages. Do you see your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date under your signature, please?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what -- is the date the 17th of February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above your signature on that same page also has your initials, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you do recall, don't you, that this statement was taken from you on the 17th of February, 1998, and that you signed it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, when you signed this statement, you believed that the statements made therein were true and correct, to the best of your knowledge and ability?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that this is correct. All it is written in English, and I do not know what it says exactly. So it would be better for me to ask me a concrete question so that I can give a complete answer, because otherwise I would not know what you are referring to and where they belong to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, that's exactly what I intend to do. I would point out, though, so there's no misunderstanding about this, as you signed in the witness acknowledgment immediately above your name on page 4, you confirmed that this statement has been read over to me in the German language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I believe that before Mr. Scott, my learned friend, gets into this questioning, he must lay a proper foundation. The proper foundation would be, Does this witness recall making this statement, number 1. Where was this statement made? What were the conditions when the statement was made? Was he under the effects of any alcohol or drugs at the time the statement was made? Who was there to take the statement from him? Was it voluntarily made? These are all foundational issues which I think must be laid before the Prosecutor can ask any specific questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you may lead your witness step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And I must say for the record, I disagree with counsel. None of those are necessary steps where I come from. Again, I can only say that. I could show the witness a red piece of cloth if it will refresh his memory, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me go back, Mr. Mrachacz. I do want to direct your attention now -- I agree with you; again, there's no mystery in the courtroom. The statement that has been put in front of you is in English. I will have to have the assistance of the interpreter, please. And I don't want you to read this out loud. The only thing I'm asking you to do is to read this to yourself. I'm going to direct your attention, with the interpreter's assistance, on page 3, and also for counsel's information, page 3, paragraph number 4, starting with the words "I heard..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to hear the interpretation or not, Your Honours, for your purposes, but I leave that in your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is it possible -- just in case this problem comes up again, is it possible that an original witness statement in the original language of the witness is retained somewhere in the Prosecution office as an exhibit as an original and can be shown in conjunction with the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It depends, Your Honour, on the nature of the statement. There is no German language statement of this document. It was taken in English, read and explained to the witness in German. With a Bosnian witness, of course, there is a statement in B/C/S. For other languages, if it was a Spanish statement or a German statement, typically, or at least often, there is no original foreign language statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So the procedure is not that the statement was taken in German and subsequently translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not consistently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And in this situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this situation, the statements were prepared in English and explained and reviewed with the witness before he signed them with an interpreter in German.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We should, in fairness, give this witness a little time with the interpreter to interpret it for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. President, normally I would have the statement withdrawn at this point so there would be no suggestion that the witness is then simply reading what has been put in front of him; but since it's in English, in this case, it probably doesn't make much difference. However, I'm going to ask the interpreter, just to avoid any suggestion, Madam Interpreter, could you assist us, please, if you would just turn the page over so that the text of that page cannot be seen by the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrachacz, reviewing that statement, has that refreshed your recollection about some additional information you know about a particular component of the Convicts' Battalion in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say the following: It is true that we operated together with other units, which were supplied with food mostly from us. And in this situation where several units were in combat together and Tuta had the supreme command, that is true. However, what they were meant to do is beyond my knowledge. I just mentioned this statement here that we sometimes were together in several units put together, and that we then had also to fight and to be supplied together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, I'm not asking to go any further than you are able to go. My question to you at the moment is not about your knowledge of orders given to this unit. So please listen to my question. Based on -- having refreshed your recollection, do you recall the name of this unit, based in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it, please?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What belongs to Mostar, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question. The name of the unit that you said just now that you operated together with and you took food to, what was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have -- I just do not know. The only unit which I know from Mostar is the Brigade Bruno Busic, because it was a major unit, and the other units I only know from hearsay and that they participated in some actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take 800 rations of food to a unit in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have not taken any supply to Mostar. When we have taken supplies to some places, that was then somewhere in the field. There were the mortar detachments from Posusje and other units, and they were supplied there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did this unit from Mostar come to Siroki Brijeg for supplies, then?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this unit then -- you said you don't recall going to Mostar. Did this unit come to Siroki Brijeg for the purposes of obtaining supplies?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this unit never came there. The point of supply was only the Park Hotel, and only our unit was supplied from this Park Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, of any ATGs in the Mostar region that were not under Tuta's command?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the units had the parts of Kaznjenicka Bojna, they were under Tuta's command. All the other units, it depended on whether they were called to us or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am going to continue. I mean I am going to move on. I'm not going to apologise for the time taken for this, because I think it was entirely appropriate. And I think a matter of procedure was important to pursue, but we have done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrachacz, I'm going to take you back to where we left off yesterday afternoon, and that is to the shelling of the mosque in Mostar. You told us that your Bofors, as you call it, was used in this action, and I ask you: At that time, do you recall other types of artillery, mortar, other than infantry rifles, just to be clear, that were used to execute this order to shell the mosque?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we have seen, there had been several guns, two Bofors, and an armoured vehicle and the mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the steps that were taken by the Bofors to target and fire at a mosque in Mostar at this time?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say, because we only saw that the mosque crumbled down. But which guns and other pieces of firing were fired on to this mosque, we weren't able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mrachacz, again I apologise. We don't seem to be communicating today, and I'm sure it's probably my fault. My question to you is not at this moment whether you saw the mosque crumble. My question to you was: The operation of your gun, can you please describe to the Chamber the steps that were taken to operate your gun to fire on the mosque, pursuant to the order that you testified under oath yesterday that Tuta gave? What steps did you take to execute that order?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to repeat that our gun had not fired at any mosque. Our command was that the infantry, which moved into Stari Most or to the old hotel or to the high school where Muslim units were hidden, that they should be fired at. At this fire-fighting with our Bofors, we first hit the wrong target, and only then we were pointed out that we should take another target. And the reason was that we had taken the wrong -- that we had installed the wrong distance into our machine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you describe to the Chamber -- let's see if we can come at it this way: Can you describe to the Chamber the amount of fire that you observed directed into Mostar following this order to destroy the mosque?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to say how much it was. I know that several Bofors, mortars. And where they were distributed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall firing 70 to 80 rounds from your Bofors at that time?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were fired from our Bofors, but not at a mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen -- and you mentioned this, but I'll just take you to this point, then. Did you see anything happen to the mosque as a result of this fire, the fire that you described generally?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only seen that the mosque was shot to pieces. But was it by tank grenades or was it by mortars, this is something I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Mrachacz, you testified yesterday, in connection with the second action at Doljani, that Tuta gave the order that no prisoners be taken. Do you recall any other instance in which a similar order was given in approximately midsummer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Mr. President and Your Honours, I believe that question misstates the evidence. I don't believe the evidence was as stated by Mr. Scott. Yesterday, I believe the testimony was that the order was that the prisoners did not need to be taken, not that they should not be taken. I think he's misstated this evidence, and I object to the question on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, maybe you could ask this question to your witness once again to make sure what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you clarify? When you gave this testimony yesterday that there should be no prisoners, how did you understand that -- what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it in that way, that this was a reaction to the loss at Cikota, and that was the only time that this order was given. As mentioned yesterday, it did not happen, because this attack was aborted before it actually had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think you answered my question in the course of saying that. But just to be clear, you don't recall a similar order being given in another action later that summer?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this order had not been then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on. Were you ever at the house or the villa where Tuta lived during your association with him?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used to be there more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask the usher's assistance, please. I'm showing you two photographs; 25.5 and 25.6, for the record. I mean either way, you can use mine or you can -- Mr. Usher, I suppose if you're not going to use those, I'll retrieve them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at, well, we can start with 25.5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually, if that can be put on the ELMO as well so everyone in the courtroom can see, unless -- I mean they are in the binders. All these documents, for everyone in the courtroom, would be in Binder 1, but again it's often easier if everyone just looks at the screen, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's depicted in the photograph marked as 25.5?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you also look at 25.6 and tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same photograph again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's not the same photograph, sir. What is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least it's the same house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us approximately how many times you were at that location?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps four or five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see persons performing labour, construction, around that property, either on the building itself or around the property in general?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the house itself, our chap who was in charge of explosions, he opened the ground by explosives. And on a ditch to be dug into the premises, there were prisoners working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what prisoners were these? I mean from what group or what army? If you can just assist us to identify who these prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know from which army or group they came, and I do not know whether they were Muslim or Serb prisoners. I only know it was a group of workers who had dug a trench or something else to put cables in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many of these prisoners did you see doing this work?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately eight to ten persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grey -- grey cloth. That was what the remnants of the Yugoslav army was, because the Muslim units did not have a uniform which was all over the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was this person that you identified earlier that was in charge of explosives. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who made the explosives, I only know his nickname. That was Stolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention forward, was the Convicts' Battalion engaged in actions at a place called Rastani in the summer or early fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were also in the surroundings of Rastani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to avoid any distractions, the photographs can be retrieved at this point. Do you recall how many times the Convicts' Battalion was engaged in action at Rastani?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly how often we were used there because this unit was what I would term as a "fire brigade," because whatever problems occurred, this unit was used. It happened that in several areas, we happened to be there three to four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And to clarify your comment just now, when you say this -- you said, "This unit was what I would term a fire brigade." First of all, which unit are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kaznjenicka Bojna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what way did you mean they were used as a fire brigade? I take it you don't mean putting out fires.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was meant that wherever there were counterattacks from the Muslim side or where the lines had been broken through and penetrated into the villages, we were used to beat them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you've just described it, then, the Convicts' Battalion was engaged at Rastani. Is that correct, then?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in command of the Convicts' Battalion at the times it was engaged at Rastani?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the battalion was in combat, the order -- the power of order was with Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During one of the actions, do you recall where your Bofors was positioned?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were usually on the hills; and while standing on the hills, we were told which position we were supposed to fire at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you which position to fire at?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said that when fire was replied from the Muslim side, we should point and target at that particular position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was at the Motorola and was in charge of the unit. It could have been an officer; and through the interpreter, we got the interpretation, this aim or that aim, and that was so for all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this, again, as you told us yesterday, was an instance where the Motorola radios were used. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall during one of these actions that the -- a field headquarters, if you will, was established very near to where the Bofors was located?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there was headquarters there, and the infantry was there, but we didn't come there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know where Tuta himself was positioned? You have told us he was in command. You know where he was positioned during this action?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say where he was present because he moved to and fro, and I do not know whether he was present in all the actions. I couldn't leave the position where I was because I had to be on the gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, will you please explain to the Chamber what you just said -- what you said just now. How was Tuta moving to and fro?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is said that he went to Mostar or to some other place. He was not always present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever know him -- let me just take your words, however. Did you ever know him to move to and fro during an action or on a battlefield?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard anything of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall him going down during one of these actions to the infantry attack himself?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, just very briefly, to an action around Prozor and Gornji Vakuf at the end of 1994. Just a couple of questions about that before we move to the final part of your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. What was the second place? I don't see it in the transcript. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, number one, this incident to which I think Mr. Scott refers is not included in this indictment, and the question itself indicates the action that took place at the end of 1994. The allegations in the indictment against Mr. Naletilic end in January of 1994. This, again, is an action that is not included in the indictment against Mr. Naletilic; and therefore, it is absolutely irrelevant. Any probative value that it might have is greatly outweighed by the prejudicial value as we are not prepared to cross-examine this witness on an issue or an incident which has never been alleged in the indictment, nor to which we have adequate facilities to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Could you please inform us where those incidents appear in the indictment? And how is it relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, it is relevant to, again, two issues in the indictment. One is superior authority, and one is the existence of an international armed conflict. I am reluctant to say more detail in light of the issues that have been raised about saying things in front of the witness. But my questions about this particular action have nothing to do, if you will, with the details of the action, but they simply-- or what happened there, other than the fact of who was in command and the presence of certain units there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Mr. President and Your Honours, again, we have no documents. We have received no documentation about this action which he wants to ask this witness. And it's all fine and good and well that he tells you why he wants to. But you know, when it comes to the fact that we will not be able to cross-examine this witness about the statement which he makes because we have not been provided the documentation concerning this incident, nor is it alleged in the indictment, it is wholly unfair. It denies Mr. Naletilic the right to a fair and just trial, and we must strongly, strongly object to this evidence coming in. It's improper, completely and wholly improper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move on very quickly this morning. To some extent, I regret these procedural issues, but I think they are important to the case, frankly, because it does have to be procedure that is followed. On these issues, Your Honour, they have had these statements. Everything I have asked this witness, everything that has been asked of this witness in the last two days, come from his witness statements which have been provided to counsel years -- months, if not years ago. Now, I don't know of any rule which says you can only ask a question based on the existence of some document that may or may not have been provided in disclosure. It has nothing to do about whether there's a document about the action -- an HVO record somewhere about the action in Prozor or Gornji Vakuf at that time. And I don't think that's the basis for a limitation on questions. I think counsel on both sides can ask questions based on what they believe the evidence is that they want to put to the witness. I don't believe there's anything about, as stated by Mr. Meek, my friend, that some documents have to be tendered about that other than the fact that it is in the witness statements that the Defence has had for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I think there has to be an end to this debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree there must be an end. I would just simply say that what my learned colleague says is true, that the Prosecutor gave us voluminous documents about everything spanning a time period of numerous events. But just because he gave us some documents doesn't mean that we would be prepared to cross-examine, because we would have no knowledge that the questions would be put to any witnesses about events that were not alleged in the indictment. And that's our point. It's improper, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you get the statement of this witness before this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, we had the statement of this witness before this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that it is all in the documents that the Prosecutor mentioned concerning these very incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The documents that this Prosecutor mentions are not only the 17 binders which have been tendered. There are many more documents than what we have. For example, we have many witness statements that may discuss things that happened in 1991 or in 1995 or in 1994, but that doesn't mean just because we have a witness statement that talks about an event that is not contained in our indictment, that we are going to track down every document that goes to that point because it was not alleged in the indictment. It is not fair to allege certain events in the indictment against our client and then come in to court and have witnesses testify about facts that are not included in the indictment and which we did not prepare for. And that is my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is there any relevance in this witness's statement concerned with this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I will just simply say it again. One of the issues in this case that the Defence has not agreed to, and we've asked them to make certain agreements and admit certain facts a number of times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott. Before you go into that, just two simple things and then we'll have a debate that may not be necessary. I think you misunderstood the learned President. The point Mr. Meek is making and the Trial Chamber is making: Is there reference to this incident which you describe in Prozor at the end of 1994 in this witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's where all this information comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's what we're concerned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And if we accept and Mr. Meek accepts that reference to it is in this witness's statement, then we'd ask you to address us on its relevance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. I appreciate that assistance. It is in the statement. Your Honour, just to be clear, this witness has provided three witness statements. They've all been provided to the Defence, as I indicated, some time ago. Virtually everything that I put to this witness in the last two days, as I'm sure the Chamber -- I think the Chamber will understand, are based on the statements that he gave, including this incident at Prozor, and Gornji Vakuf and many others. In response to the second question, Judge Clark: The relevance of it again is that the Defence have put in issue the superior authority and command responsibility of, in this case, Tuta. Now, we are going to put on a lot of evidence -- we're going to try -- we're going to try to tender a lot of evidence to prove his command responsibility for actions committed by the Convicts' Batallion and his subordinates, for which it is and will be the Prosecutor's position that he should be held responsible under Article 7(3) of the Statute as superior responsibility. We have tendered, through this witness, a number of pieces of evidence of what we would submit clearly demonstrates Tuta's extensive command and control over the Convicts' Battalion, and a number of incidents, some specifically named in the indictment, others not specifically named in the indictment. Again, so that there is no misunderstanding or lest the Prosecution be accused of being sneaky in some way, this one is not in the indictment. It's not in the indictment, but it is an incident covered by the time period in this case, which again goes to the fact that Tuta commanded this unit in the field, that he gave orders. That's relevance number 1. Relevance number 2: That there were elements of the army of the Republic of Croatia engaged in this same action. It goes to the issue of the existence of international armed conflict, which is directly relevant to proving the charges of grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. So it's relevant in both those ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: After hearing the arguments put forward by both sides, this Chamber believes that this issue is relevant in the indictment. Firstly, it's concerned with the command responsibilities and, second, that is the international armed conflict which we would like to hear. So long as the Defence counsel has already received the statement of this witness. The objection from Mr. Meek is overruled. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, please listen to my questions, because I'm going to ask you only very specific things about this action. First of all, you do recall, do you not, the Convicts' Battalion being deployed in the area of Prozor and Gornji Vakuf in late 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge -- who gave the briefing and gave the orders to deploy?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order came from Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in command of that action?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who had the supreme command. It was in the surroundings of Vakuf, and it was not only us but there were other units also present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that assist. And over all those units - and I don't mean who was somewhere else, someone that was in Mostar, someone that was in Zagreb - who in the field had command over this group of units engaged on the HVO side in that action?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All units who had come down from the Siroki Brijeg and Mostar area were under the command of Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall, during that action, whether there were military components from another army who were also present at that time?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were units from the HV from Croatia present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those units?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember that the Tiger Brigades were there - they were the most known ones - and the units from the area of Prozor. But they were under a different command. That was a former commander of the Legion who was in the power of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just so the record is clear, who was that for that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not know under whose command they were. Some of them even acted independently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Of the units that you have told us about in the last two days, Mr. Mrachacz, did you ever hear of a unit called the "Vinko Skrobo ATG"?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of that name and of this unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who the commander of that unit was?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether that unit was part of the Convicts' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is beyond my knowledge. These units changed permanently and they changed their names. Therefore, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever know an ATJ - excuse me - an ATJ -- sorry, Your Honours -- an ATG named "Mrmak"?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely not known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrmak, that's what -- okay. I just wanted to be clear which question you were then further responding to. Mr. Mrachacz, you told us yesterday that there were two rules or orders that Tuta had given in connection with military discipline. I told you the second one we would come back to. I believe you said - and I'm sure you'll correct me and I'm sure counsel will correct me if I'm wrong - that the second rule was that if someone wanted to leave the Kaznjenicka Bojna and join the Muslim side, that they should be killed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave that order or stated that rule?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order came from Tuta and was related mostly to foreigners, because none of the Croats were to desert to the Muslim units, the reason being that by the end of '92, five British changed sides and to change to the Muslim units which were fighting against the Croat units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of a time when Tuta himself was engaged in executing any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask one other question about that. Again, I'm being very clear about what I'm doing to see if it prompts his memory. If it doesn't, then that's the last question I will ask about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall any incident in front of or near the Ministry of Defence in Mostar, where two prisoners were killed?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where you are driving at, but I know this matter only from hearsay. And this is why I said just now that I do not know anything about it myself, because I do not pay any attention to hearsay. I haven't seen it myself. And the source who has told me was a gentleman called "Simang," and I do not know whether he told me the correct thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. And in fact that was my only other question was: What you're saying is you heard this from someone named "Simang"?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know another German mercenary member of the Convicts' Battalion named - and I'll probably say this wrong - "Braunreuter"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not understand the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me spell it, and perhaps you can help me. B-R-U-A-N-R-E-U-T-E-R.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not spelled out here. B-R-U-A?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: B-R-A-U-N-R-E-U-T-E-R.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Braunreuter," that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he? Just explain to the Chamber, by way of background, who was this person?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Braunreuter was an Austrian, a member of our unit, and he was also accommodated in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask the Chamber's indulgence. I'm about to finish, but I think if we launch into an area now, it will undoubtedly not be completed before the break, and it's something that I would ask not to have to interrupt in the middle of, if I could, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So do you suggest that we break right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, before you start, the registrar has something to tell us about arrangements of the trials for the first week of October.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There has been a lot of speculation and questions about the calendar for the first week of October, so I would just like to confirm that there will be no hearings for the first week of October, and we resume the following week, which is, I believe, the 8th. Let me just check to make sure. The 1st through the 5th, we are not in session, and that's because other hearings have been scheduled, and there's other matters, court maintenance and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we are on that topic now, just two things to confirm: Just so there's no uncertainty about that, based on that, please understand the Prosecution, of course, will not arrange, then, for witnesses to be travelling that week. So we will take that as a done deal. Mr. President, secondly, on the week of the 8th, as long as we're on scheduling, we're not objecting to it necessarily, but just by clarification, we are down on the 8th and 9th of October in Courtroom III in what some have called the afternoon or evening session from 2.15 p.m. to 7.00 in the evening. Is that also correct? It doesn't have to be answered on the spot, but it would also be helpful to know that at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the registrar could give us a proper answer on this issue. I am also wondering about this question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm looking at the most recent calendar, which is the 14th of September. And I see hearings scheduled on Monday, October 8th in Courtroom III, from 9:30 to 4.00 for Monday and Tuesday, and then in Courtroom I Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, which is the 10th, and 11th, and 12th of October, 9.30 to 4.00. And then, of course, on Fridays, you know we adjourn at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, before the break, I asked you about this other mercenary or member of the KB, Convicts' Battalion, named Braunreuter. Did you have a conversation with this man about a person he had killed?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, please, who did he kill and why, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that in Hotel Park, there were rumours that Mr. Braunreuter, together with another French comrade, had killed -- had shot dead a 50-year-old Frenchman, together with another person. But since nothing was to be heard about that in town, I talked to a local and went to the place where we found this dead Frenchman. And whereupon that, I went to Tuta, told him about it, and he said to me that I should keep my fingers out of it. It was none of my business. So that is -- that was all for me, with the exception that I made sure that the corpse was removed because the corpse was lying in the vicinity of a church and a school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what this killed Frenchman -- and perhaps this other person that was also killed -- do you know what they were doing in Siroki Brijeg around that time or what their role was?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, the French had their own unit, and they had their own commander, and they were commanded by a person who spoke French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they had their own unit where, of what?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subordinate to our unit, but they had their own commander. It was a subunit commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying, if I understand you, sir, this was another subunit of the Kaznjenicka Bojna?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were part and parcel of the unit, but they used to have their own commander who had come from the former Croat region with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, the last thing on that point, just to try to be as clear as possible: Are you telling us that just as there were a group of German mercenaries, if you will, there were also a group of French members of the Convicts' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot say exactly like that. This group came as a close group from Croatia, from the -- from Slovenia, where they had operated, and they came down to Herzegovina. And in this group, there were several Frenchmen, four or five of them, and one German, and this group was then distributed to the entire unit. They were not an independent mercenary group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But they were fighting on the side of the HVO, I take it.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're saying just now - and again I'm only trying to make the record as clear as possible - they were disbursed through the Convicts' Battalion, so they were not a unit, as such?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were no longer a unit. They were distributed to the various areas, depending on what knowledge they had about weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know whether this French person who was killed, was he among this group of Frenchmen? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had come with this group. But what else has happened or so, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Braunreuter tell you on whose order or direction he had killed this Frenchman?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't let me know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had the corpse in fact been laying near the church in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been approximately one week, because the smell was already very sharp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long was it between your first hearing about this from Braunreuter to the time that you told us that you went to Tuta about it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After it turned out that it was true, that a corpse was lying there, I addressed him immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that he said anything to you other than to essentially keep your nose out of it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only thing he says, just, "Keep your fingers out of it. This is none of your business."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, the reason that you are serving a prison sentence in the country where you're serving that sentence at this time, that was in connection with killing two men in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I shot dead only one man, and he was a deserter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me. Did you in fact shoot and kill this man that you just described as a deserter?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, on whose orders did you shoot this man?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to -- I have to rely here on the command given -- on the order given by Tuta, which was: When you have a deserter in front of you, you've got to shoot him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us anything more about exactly what Tuta told you to do in connection with this man?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He himself didn't say anything to myself because I didn't meet him on that day. What was decisive for me was the standing order that when there are deserters on their way to leave our unit, they are to be shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone else participate in this killing with you?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simang was together there with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the man who was killed?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference to both the Frenchman who was killed that you told us about a few minutes ago and the killing of this man, the man that you and Simang killed, to your knowledge was any member of the Convicts' Battalion disciplined or punished for either of those individuals being killed?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever disciplined or punished by Tuta for killing the man you killed?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examinations? Mr. Seric. Sorry, Mr. Krsnik. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're just trying to serve the rules, when one lawyer gets up on his feet to object, that he is the one who is to continue. But when it comes to the cross-examination, we shuffle things around. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. My name is Kresimir Krsnik. I represent Mr. Mladen Naletilic. I'm going to ask you a number of questions, and I'm going to try to frame them in such a way that we receive very short answers from you. I am going to base them on what you personally have experienced and seen, in other words, your own personal experience, knowledge. So let me start with the first question. The famous statement of 17 February, 1998, I see at the top that your Defence counsel was present. He was needed because you were faced with some accusations?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these accusations --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can we please go in the private session, because we happen to know the list of upcoming witnesses, and I want to avoid my learned colleagues objecting, and I don't know what that witness's protective measures are going to be. So for these two questions, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you be so kind and tell me, did someone from among your fellow German co-combatants give any statements to German Television and receive payment for that?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those statements false or were they self-promoting, in terms of people praise their own contribution, and you disagreed with it because you called him up on that?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was to give an interview in Berlin in a TV station called "SAT-1," but we insisted that he will bring along a complete cassette where everything had been recorded with all the previous and the aftermath discussions. And from this, it could be seen that he placed this person in the foreground, which led to controversies amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this broadcast, the German authorities launched some investigations, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that it happened and started exactly like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person in question, is that the same question that we referred to during the private session?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's Mr. Falk Simang.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a person who was given to lies and fabrications?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about this report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person gave a number of false statements to the German police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know which statements he had made there. I wouldn't be able to give you any information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to the ones that were read out during your trial.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say the following: Shortly before the trial came to Germany, I came to Germany and I had no real insight in the statements made by Mr. Simang.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were not read during your joint trial?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Simang refused to make statements on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your lawyers did not alert you to those?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was just a show trial there, this case, and things which I mentioned, for example, that was a regular unit, that was just -- I was just blamed of making some protective allegations from my side, and the other statements were rejected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going into the merits of the sentence; I was just going to ask you, because in the materials that I received from this trial, this is what is stated, his statements that he gave to the German police. That is the basis of my question. And that is because in his statement, that is, his statement was part of the basis for the sentence against you, which is life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not received anything of his statement except for those parts which concerned me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you received a life sentence?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
