utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that this was a show trial or that you were framed in some way?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had -- one could have the impression. I had not seen any lawyer, for example, until three weeks before the trial started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did the German police come to Croatia and did an interview there?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Tuta also there with you?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that you had to surrender to the German authorities or that you would be tried in Croatia or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuta had made an application to the German authorities: If they follow up these investigations, they should make an application with the Mostar Ministry of Defence, and they would deal with that there. But I didn't make this application. As time went by, the pressure from the German authorities was becoming bigger and bigger. Then I had a conversation with Tuta, and he told me in this situation, it would be better if I were to give in myself to the authorities; that because of the situation, the man in question was a deserter, that the sentence could not be more than two or three, or three or four years. And that was then after this conversation that I gave myself in to the German authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you confirm the fact that Tuta was one of the key persons, key figures, in your surrendering to the German authorities, because you did that of your own free will, because you eventually went there?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question: When you're suspected of such serious crimes, who else can take such decisions except for a Court?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not clear. What I really wanted to ask is, and in light of the response you gave to my learned friend, could Tuta at all punish such crimes when there is suspicion of such crime, and if -- it's a different situation if somebody had confessed. But is this the type of crime that he could have decided on, or was this a matter for the police and judiciary?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now say whether you have any knowledge about the man, the Frenchman who was found dead? Do you have any personal knowledge whether there was any investigation conducted on this and whether there were any court proceedings launched against anyone in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing is known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrachacz, can you now please tell me, who was present when you gave your statement on the 17th of February and the statement that we're discussing here? And how did this -- how was this interview conducted? Let me ask you first this: Did you sign the English version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only signed the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This English version was translated to you into German, and that's when you signed it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you 100 percent sure that everything that you actually said was translated in such manner into English?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened that during translations, only the content was translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether some of the questions that were asked of you were made into the text, and then the interpreter incorporated them into your answers?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude that everything that you said in German -- that everything that you said in German was directly translated into English and put in the record?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever take the English version and gave it to your own translator to check on the quality of translation?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude that to date, you have not conducted -- carried out a control of your statement in English?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied on what was translated back to me into German. That means I relied on the translation of all the pages which were translated back into German to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the German and English languages have the same structure and same rules?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you no clue -- I have no clue, as far as this is concerned, because I do not know any English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have Croatian names, and then you have them translated into German, and then they are translated on into English. Can you tell me how you managed all that?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Croatian names are concerned, I of course pronounced them. But whether they have been correctly transliterated or correctly written, that's of course a matter I would not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence has noticed a number of these mistakes. I'm just going to give you one example. The general in Vrgorac whom you mentioned, you said that his name was "Daidza"?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, in all your statements that you had given to the Prosecution investigators, and in a transcript that is all compiled here, had it not been for the Defence and its clarification of the issue, this person would probably have gone down in history as "Deitscher." And were the Defence not concerned about the truth of the facts here, you would probably have gone on believing that you have met with a person who in fact doesn't exist, a Croatian general who simply does not exist. Mr. Mrachacz, is it clear to you now why I ask you this question? Because in the transcript of your statement with this Tribunal, it states that you went and saw a General Deitscher.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I only know that his name was "Deitscher," at least he was called like that; an elderly gentleman, he was more than 70 years old, and he was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. And in fact his name is "Daidza" or his nickname is "Daidza," D-A-I-D-Z-A. My question to you is: Can you say that the statements that you have given in English are 100 per cent correct, or are they correct at all?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I can't read the translation into English and I do not know in which way it is translated, so I have to rely on -- the way it is written is exactly as I have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we have elucidated the matter enough. Can you please tell me now, while we're at it, we're discussing Mr. Daidza, was he a Muslim; that is, was he a Croat of Muslim faith, or was he an ethnic Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say he belonged to the Muslim faith, but I could not say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me about that unit of which he was the commander, this general, and to which you belonged, according to your statement? Did it train Muslims, did it arm Muslims and, together with them, assisted them in 1992 in the war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the following on that: This unit was composed 50 per cent of Croats and 50 per cent of Bosniaks. There was a second commander, but I would not know this person's name. And when struggling in the -- when fighting in the barracks at Capljina, mostly Croats were used and were in combat and not Muslims. And therefore there was a mighty fight between the two commanders, between Deitscher and the commander of the Croats, so that this unit then separated. The one went to the Bosnian area, and the unit of the Croats then moved to the direction, if I'm not mistaken, between Ljubuski -- anywhere around in the area around Ljubuski. That was a holiday camp which they then used as their bases. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Daidza was a general of the Croatian army - and I'm referring now to the State of Croatia - and the unit you just referred to was a unit of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the war against the Serbs, it was quite natural that the Croatian army would assist Muslims in training, arming, and that they would also die for the cause of liberating this area?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had weapons, and they were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. My question did not enter in the record in its entirety. The unit that you referred to, it was quite natural that it fought against the Serbs, and that the Croats would die for the liberation of the ethnic areas inhabited by Muslims to liberate them from the Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can answer with yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please tell me, if you can, do you know that there was also an agreement reached between the Muslims and Croats about this at the highest state level because at that time, the State of Bosnia did not yet exist?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether there had been agreements, I couldn't tell -- I wouldn't be not in the know about it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I am just trying to verify. Perhaps you know, even though in the beginning I advised you that my questions to you would be about your personal, first-hand knowledge rather than something that you know second- or third-hand. Can you tell me, to your knowledge - and we're, again, using this unit because you knew something about that - did the Croatian State arm equally the Croats and the Muslims and train them equally, fed them equally, armed them equally, and that Muslims from different parts of Bosnia asked for assistance on a daily basis? And I'm talking about the aggression of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just inquire, is this witness being asked about Convicts' Battalion, or are these just general, historical matters? I think some foundation would have to be laid if he's voicing opinions about matters beyond the scope of the Convicts' Battalion of which he was a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that that's a reasonable question. Maybe you could clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, that question would be reasonable if I did not know the indictment and if I had not heard my learned colleague's questions, which went on for over five hours. The question was whether there were taking off HV patches, putting on HVO patches, so they are talking about the Croatian aggression. And my colleague should know at least about the Split agreements. So I am within the ambit of the questions, as my learned friend. Unfortunately, I have a good memory and remember everything that he said, and I know the indictment by heart. And if the Croatian army has carried out an aggression, let's see what kind of aggression that was. Let's ask this witness about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the question is very simple: Is this witness being asked about Convicts' Battalion, or are these just general, historical matters? You have to give some guidance on this issue. And Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just what you said. I'm sorry. I'm not questioning -- I have no comments on counsel's memory. But if the question is -- it's not what I said or what's at issue in the indictment. This witness can't talk about every issue in the indictment and what the agreements may have been between Tudjman and somebody else. He was a member of the Convicts' Battalion. I completely agree that counsel is fully entitled to ask him questions about that and the practices in that battalion. Were there Muslims members in that unit? Were they treated fairly? He can ask about those things if it's within his knowledge. But these questions are just simply questions about the war. It could be anywhere in the former Yugoslavia. I don't think it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's just see where Defence counsel is going to lead us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor, if I follow it correctly, asked questions about 1992 for about two-and-a-half hours. That's historical background, and the witness answered to best of his knowledge. The Defence is doing nothing different. Remember, I just asked him a moment ago, "if you know," because if I understand it correctly, the gentleman had spent a significant period of time in Croatia. And I am just relying on the part of examination in chief that the Prosecution has conducted. So General Daidza, Vrgorac, Croatian Army, all this was there. And we are trying to also contribute to the full picture of this, because it would not be fair if the Trial Chamber only relied on the picture produced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have already given you the leeway to continue. You just pursue that question to make things more clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise. I thought that I was going to still respond to the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We left off at the last question where we corrected the transcript. And let me sort of abbreviate the question. You then gave me the answer in the affirmative, and then I asked you whether there was equal treatment, equal arming during 1992 and during the fighting against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the units had the same payment, the same weaponry, the same accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived in Croatia at that time. Did you personally see Muslim refugees who were as a result of the Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more than enough. The whole military camp near to Split, Baska Voda, was full with Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian State cared for them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please answer this: When you talked about your trip to Ljubuski, was this in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was early '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when UNPROFOR appeared in Croatia, in what year?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please tell me, the General Daidza's unit was named "Tomislav" or "King Tomislav," and it has nothing to do with the town called Tomislavgrad. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Tomislav is due to the first Croatian king, and the town of Tomislavgrad has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were in General Daidza's unit, you never went to the town called Tomislavgrad, and this town is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please tell me, in order to be able to tell this Trial Chamber what "HOS" stands for, can you say that?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: HOS is the military wing of the Croatian party HSP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness, but the Trial Chamber does not know what "HSP" is. It is "Croatian Party of Rights." Let me help you on this.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exactly translate what it -- what the exact translation is. But at any rate, it is a right-wing party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And HOS was its military wing?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that period, 1991 and 1992, did an army exist at all in Croatia by the name of "Croatian army" in 1991, even in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not ask my question properly. Was it in the process of establishment? Before '91, did the Croatian army exist? I thought perhaps we could just go straight to that question.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that was before 1991, I wouldn't know. What I understand is that at that time, one could not speak of a well-formed army as you would usually have in Europe. At that time, it was just a structurisation that several units of combat units were being tried to be put together. But one could not speak about a structurised army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other military organisations like HOS, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, let me try to clarify it for you. If somebody had a lot of money and was a foreign donor from the Croatian emigration or from Croatia itself, could they establish their own unit, provided they were able to equip it and arm it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you had enough financial means and if you had the means to equip them with weaponry, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Usually such a person would also become a commander of such unit; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something similar also take place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 in the war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether people formed units privately is the thing I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the light of your military experience, can you tell me -- and in the light of these private units, if we can call them that, but in the light of their desire to defend themselves against the Serb aggression, who was in the position to control them at all?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the units operated independently, they were then under the command of the crisis headquarters which were established or any other headquarters. One could not say at that moment. Only at a later stage they were structurised, and by that time they just could not operate -- they could not work that in such an operative manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And crisis staffs were established for protection of civilian population and for military self-organisation. They mostly consisted of civilians without any military experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were only civilians, I do not know, because people did not walk about in uniforms, so you couldn't say is the person a civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every person who bought a uniform for his own money, or acquired a Kalashnikov or any other type of weapon for his own money, could join any unit, because at that time these units mostly consisted or almost exclusively consisted of volunteers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would say that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge that in Croatia and in Herzegovina, people did arm themselves?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing is known to me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: In Croatia during 1992, the HOS became part of the HV, but with significant difficulties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've heard of that. There was also an explosive attack at the HOS headquarters in Zagreb, near the railway station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these were attempts to create some kind of an army; was that the objective?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not know, because I had been there only for a very short period, three to four weeks or so altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during that period when you were in Zagreb, did the head of that party, because he was unwilling to subordinate to the Croatian army and was actually opposed to the creation of the Croatian army, ended up in prison and was investigated, and you were his bodyguard or driver - I'm not exactly sure - but you were in the entourage of Mr. Paraga?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing was known to us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And again as I advised you in the beginning, I only want to know what you know personally. We have ten minutes left, and I would like to use the time to show the witness a photograph. And I would like cooperation from the Registry and Mr. Usher, if the following exhibit can be placed on the ELMO. Just a moment, Your Honours, if you will indulge me. Exhibit P11, page 17. It's a photograph of the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have the photograph in front of you. Can you recognise what is it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; that's the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a complete picture of it? Can all structures be seen, or are there some missing?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's only part of it. It's the building where the ATG were housed. That's the light buildings. And the building in the background, which is also of a light colour, that is where the former training rooms which were not used in my days there, the rooms for training people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, can you see in this picture where you, yourself, were billeted? You said that you were at the Heliodrom. And what period of time was it when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher has a pointer, so you can use that.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, could you please describe it.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you mean, the building, to describe the building?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, Witness, you see, we only have a picture here. It's an image, and we need words.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a three-storey building that was meant for housings of officers or pilots. That was also usually rooms for one person. They were very well preserved. And that is because of this well preservation, this good preservation, that our units moved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What is the location of the building in this picture?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building is at the -- towards the end of the complex, just short of the hangars and the other buildings which follow in the further direction, in the direction further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me the colour, and then the shape, what is it, elongated; is the roof different colour than the walls? And looking from left to right, is it the first, second, third building? These are some of the things I'm asking you to describe.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this perspective, it's the building with the white roof on the right-hand side. Then there is a free area and something like a sports ground. And the building I'm describing is the building where we were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that is sufficient to be clear on which building it is. I'm going to try to give you a separate copy in due course, which you can then mark. I do not want to put markings on the Prosecutor's copy, but now we've at least established what building that was. In this area -- and I don't know whether we can see it in this photograph. Perhaps on Monday, we can show you some other photographs. There were several HVO units, several different HVO units that were billeted there; is that correct, throughout the Heliodrom? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the entire Heliodrom, there were several units. But in this building completely, there was only one unit of ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand that. But I'm going a bit wider. There were several units at the Heliodrom. It is clear about this building that -- I think we have cleared up.

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several units there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were recruits also brought there? Was there any training conducted there, and were the home guards also there?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training was also conducted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I can't see well from this vantage point, but I believe it is 1.00, and I think that I have concluded with this one area of questioning. And I would then continue on Monday, if it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. There's two things I want to mention: First, Witness, I have to warn you, as I do with all the witnesses, please do not speak to anybody about your evidence until your testimony has been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. completed, and do not let anybody speak to you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And there are some procedure matters that will be announced by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to inform everyone, the Vasiljevic case will be sitting in here next, so please take out all of your belongings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 9.30 Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
